sweep_summary: Two title-hits for Choctaw, both already in the per-language bibliography. Lombardi & McCarthy 1991 (Phonology 8) was obtained as the full open author manuscript from McCarthy's UMass page (previously known to the catalog only as 'ms' page references) and read: it states that stress prominence is not a feature of Choctaw phonetics, that the metrical system is iambic (diagnosed by Alternate/Rhythmic Lengthening of even-numbered light syllables), and that word accent is a lexically unpredictable high tone on some words and morphological grades, following Nicklas 1974 — confirming the catalog's 'tonal' (pitch accent) coding from Broadwell 2006 without superseding it. Munro & Ulrich 1984 (WCCFL 3, pp. 191-202) is the primary source on the iambic rhythmic-lengthening rule and its cyclic application (known here only via L&M 1991); no open copy exists anywhere probed (IA, HathiTrust, CORE, Crossref, S2, OpenAlex, Bing/DDG, UCLA page) — library print only, medium priority since Ulrich 1986 and Broadwell 2006 restate its content. Nothing in this search of works with stress in the title contradicts the catalog.

new_statements.quote: Although stress prominence does not seem to be a feature of Choctaw phonetics, the language nevertheless has the typical characteristics of an iambic metrical system. Evidence of iambicity comes from the properties of the rule of Alternate Lengthening (Nicklas 1974: 117f.; 1975: 242f.; Munro and Ulrich 1984; Ulrich 1986: 53ff.). In a sequence of monomoraic syllables, every even-numbered syllable, counting from the left, lengthens its vowel. [...] According to Nicklas (1974: 12), accent in Choctaw is an unpredictable property of some words or morphological patterns. It is realized by high tone.

new_statements.reading: Choctaw has no phonetic stress prominence; its metrical organization is a left-to-right iambic foot whose only surface exponent is rhythmic vowel lengthening of even-numbered light syllables (never word-final). Word-level prominence proper is a lexically unpredictable high-tone accent borne by some words and by certain morphological grades, i.e. a pitch accent/tonal system, not a stress system. This confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2009. How (not) to do phonological typology: the case of pitch accent. Language Sciences 31(2-3): 213-238. doi:10.1016/j.langsci.2008.12.007. [Open preprint: UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report (2007): 654-685, doi:10.5070/p74hb059t7]
tone_statements.quote: Another problem is distinguishing what would be an obligatory H “accent” from an obligatory H boundary tone. In Choctaw [Muskogean; Oklahoma], every word ends in a /H/ tone (Ulrich 1989:163). In addition, some words also have an additional /HL/ assigned to either their antepenultimate or penultimate syllable. As a result, words may have the shapes Ln-H, Ln-H-L-H or Ln-H-LH (the last having undergone a rule whereby final HL-H → H-LH). This produces a system where the final /H/ is obligatory, and the additional /HL/ culminative. Since the two can co-occur, Choctaw words potentially violate OBLIG(H).

tone_statements.summary: Obligatory word-final H (boundary tone) + culminative /HL/ on penult/antepenult of some words; melodies Ln-H, Ln-H-L-H, Ln-H-LH.
